content.title: About
content.content: Beef curry is a fragrant Indian dish in which tender pieces of beef are simmered in a sauce made from tomatoes, onions, garlic, ginger, and spices such as turmeric, cumin, coriander, garam masala, and chili. The dish has a rich, slightly spicy flavor and is often served with rice or flatbreads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Curry originated in South India, where local spices and meat were combined.
The word “curry” comes from the Tamil word “kari,” meaning sauce.
Beef is traditionally cooked slowly in curry to become tender and absorb the spice aromas.
Regional variations are wide: in Kerala coconut milk is added, while in Punjab yogurt is common.
Curry became popular in Western countries after the colonial era and has been adapted to local tastes.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef supplies easily absorbed heme iron, important for blood formation and energy.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Turmeric and other spices contain polyphenols with anti‑inflammatory and antioxidant properties.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Ginger and garlic stimulate gastric secretions, aiding digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef is rich in vitamin B12 and other B‑vitamins that support the nervous system.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Some cuts of beef can be high in saturated fat, so choosing lean cuts is advisable.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Individuals may have allergic reactions to turmeric, cumin, or other spices.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain salt; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portions.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Beef must be cooked thoroughly to avoid salmonella and other pathogens.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot beef curry with steamed basmati rice, couscous, or Indian flatbreads such as naan or roti. Garnish with fresh cilantro, a dollop of yogurt, or a squeeze of lime for extra brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.

cereal-or-granola-bar-general-mills-natu.title: Nature Valley Sweet and Salty Granola Bar

content.title: About
content.content: Nature Valley Sweet and Salty Granola Bar is a crunchy, whole‑grain snack bar coated with a sweet‑salty glaze. Made by General Mills, it is designed for on‑the‑go snacking. Each bar weighs about 42 g and contains oats, sunflower oil, honey, sugar and salt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bar is made of two baked oat halves that are glued together with a glaze.
The combination of honey sweetness and sea‑salt creates the signature “sweet‑salty” flavor popular in the US.
It was first introduced in the 1970s as part of the Nature Valley line aimed at active lifestyles.
Whole oat flakes are used rather than milled flour, preserving a hearty texture.
The product contains no artificial colors or flavors.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: Oats provide complex carbohydrates that release energy slowly, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Modest protein content
items.content: Oats and sunflower oil supply about 3 g of protein per bar, useful for muscle repair.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Sunflower oil adds polyunsaturated fatty acids that are beneficial for heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Oats are a source of thiamine (B1) and niacin (B3), which play roles in energy metabolism.

items.title: Gluten sensitivity
items.content: The bar contains oats, which are often processed on shared equipment with wheat, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Each bar contains roughly 9 g of sugar, which may be a concern for those monitoring sugar intake.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: The bar has about 0.3 g of salt, which can add up for individuals watching sodium consumption.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: At approximately 190 kcal per bar, portion control is advisable for calorie‑restricted diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bar straight from the package as a quick snack. It can be chopped and added to yogurt, kefir or muesli for extra crunch, or used as a crunchy layer in dessert parfaits.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bars in their original packaging in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal the package tightly to prevent moisture absorption, which can make the bars soft.

content.title: About
content.content: Garlic bread is a fragrant slice of bread topped with a mixture of butter, minced garlic, herbs, and sometimes cheese. It is commonly served in fast‑food outlets and restaurants as an appetizer or side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first garlic‑bread recipe appeared in Italy in the early 1920s.
Garlic bread became popular in the United States in the 1970s thanks to chain pizzerias.
There is a “black” garlic bread version that incorporates cuttlefish ink into the dough.
Garlic bread is often served with marinara or cheese sauce for dipping.
Vegan versions replace butter with plant‑based margarine.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Garlic contains allicin and other compounds that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports immune function
items.content: Regular consumption of garlic may boost the body’s natural defenses.

items.title: May lower cholesterol
items.content: Studies suggest garlic can help reduce LDL (bad) cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates and energy
items.content: The bread provides a quick source of energy through its carbs.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Bread supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Wheat allergy or gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid traditional garlic bread.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Butter and added salt make it fairly salty; those with hypertension should limit portions.

items.title: Gas and digestive discomfort
items.content: Garlic can cause bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Butter and bread make the dish calorie‑rich, so moderation is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Garlic bread is usually served hot, cut into triangles. It can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, used for dipping into sauces, or as a side to soups, salads, and pasta dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a bag for up to 2 months. Reheat before serving and ensure the bread has not dried out.

content.title: About
content.content: Ginger is the rhizome of the plant Zingiber officinale, native to Southeast Asia. It has a pungent, warming, slightly sweet and citrusy flavor. Ginger is used fresh, dried, ground, and pickled, and is added to tea, soups, sauces, baked goods, and Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The edible part of ginger is not a root but a rhizome, an underground stem of the plant.
Ginger is related to turmeric and cardamom.
Gingerols give ginger its heat; when dried, they partly turn into the more pungent shogaols.
Pickled ginger is traditionally served with sushi.
India and China are among the largest producers of ginger.

items.title: May reduce nausea
items.content: Ginger is studied as a remedy for nausea, including motion sickness and nausea during pregnancy.

items.title: Contains gingerols
items.content: Gingerols and other compounds in ginger have antioxidant properties.

items.title: May support digestion
items.content: Ginger is traditionally used to ease discomfort and heaviness after meals.

items.title: Anti-inflammatory properties
items.content: Compounds in ginger are being studied for anti-inflammatory effects, but evidence is still limited.

items.title: Adds flavor without calories
items.content: A small amount of ginger makes dishes flavorful with practically no extra calories.

items.title: Heartburn
items.content: In large amounts, ginger may cause heartburn and stomach irritation.

items.title: Effect on blood clotting
items.content: Large amounts of ginger may affect blood clotting; people taking anticoagulants or facing surgery should consult a doctor.

items.title: Gallstones
items.content: Ginger may increase bile flow, so people with gallstones should check with a doctor.

items.title: Supplements and medications
items.content: Concentrated ginger supplements, especially during pregnancy or alongside blood pressure or diabetes medications, should be discussed with a doctor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh ginger can be grated or sliced and added to tea, soups, sauces, marinades, vegetable and meat dishes, and baked goods. The skin is easy to scrape off with a spoon. Much less ground ginger is needed than fresh, and its flavor is different.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh ginger in the refrigerator, wrapped in paper or in a container, where it keeps for two to three weeks. For longer storage, freeze it whole or grated. Keep ground ginger in an airtight jar in a cool, dark place. Discard the root if it becomes soft, shriveled, or moldy.

hot-dog-sandwich-meat-and-poultry-on-whi.title: Hot Dog Sandwich, Meat and Poultry, on White Bun

content.title: About
content.content: A hot dog is a sandwich consisting of a cooked meat‑and‑poultry sausage placed in a split white bun. It is a staple of fast‑food cuisine and is commonly served with mustard, ketchup, mayonnaise, and various toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial hot dog appeared in the United States in the late 19th century.
The soft white bun softens the flavor of the sausage and holds sauces better than a harder roll.
In some U.S. regions the hot dog is colloquially called a “papa‑john” or “papa‑johnny.”
There are more than 30 varieties of hot‑dog sausages, including beef, pork, turkey and chicken blends.
In 2012 the United States recorded a consumption record of over 20 million hot dogs per day.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Meat‑and‑poultry sausage provides high‑quality protein needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat in the sausage is a good source of heme iron, which helps prevent anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product is rich in B12, B6 and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: A hot dog delivers a fast‑acting calorie boost, useful when time is limited.

items.title: Carbohydrates from the bun
items.content: The white bun supplies simple carbs that are quickly converted to usable energy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed sausages often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Meat sausages may be high in saturated fat, contributing to elevated cholesterol levels.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some varieties contain nitrites and other preservatives that are considered unsafe in excess.

items.title: Allergy to food additives
items.content: Spices and flavorings used in the sausage can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High glycemic index of the bun
items.content: A white bun has a high glycemic index, which can cause a rapid spike in blood sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the hot dog hot, splitting the bun lengthwise and placing the sausage inside. Add mustard, ketchup, mayonnaise, pickles, onions, cheese or chili to taste. It is commonly paired with french fries, a side salad or a soft drink.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the sausage refrigerated at +2…+4 °C, and a prepared hot dog in an airtight container for no more than 2 hours at room temperature. Store the bun in a dry place, preferably in a paper bag, to prevent it from becoming soggy.

oatmeal-instant-plain-made-with-non-dair.title: Instant Oatmeal, Plain, Made with Non‑Dairy Milk, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Instant oatmeal is made from whole oat flakes that have been processed to cook quickly when mixed with hot liquid. This version is prepared with non‑dairy milk (soy, almond, or oat) and contains no added fat, making it low‑calorie and suitable for weight‑watching diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown for over 5,000 years.
Instant oatmeal retains most of the fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals found in whole oats.
Oats contain beta‑glucan, a soluble fiber known to lower cholesterol.
Preparing without added fat makes the product ideal for low‑calorie eating plans.
Oatmeal can be customized with fruit, nuts, spices, or sweeteners to suit any taste.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains beta‑glucan
items.content: Beta‑glucan can reduce LDL (bad) cholesterol and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Provides steady, long‑lasting energy without rapid glucose spikes.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B5, and folate aid energy metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: No added fat makes it suitable for low‑fat and calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to oats or to the avenin protein they contain.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can bind minerals and reduce their absorption; pairing oatmeal with vitamin‑C‑rich foods can mitigate this.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Oats are often processed on equipment shared with wheat, so gluten‑sensitive individuals should choose certified gluten‑free oats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Combine 40 g of oatmeal with 200 ml of hot non‑dairy milk, stir, and let stand for 1–2 minutes. Add fresh berries, sliced fruit, honey, or spices such as cinnamon or vanilla if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a cool, dry place away from direct light. After opening, reseal tightly or transfer to an airtight container. Follow the “best before” date printed on the packaging.

content.title: About
content.content: Parsnip is a root vegetable from the Apiaceae family, native to the Mediterranean and Western Asia. When cooked it develops a sweet, nutty flavor and a tender texture. Cooked parsnip is commonly used in purees, soups, casseroles, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Parsnip was popular in ancient Rome and was considered more valuable than carrots.
Sugar content increases during storage, making older roots sweeter.
Parsnip contains more beta‑carotene than carrots, though it remains pale in color.
In Russia parsnip is often called “carrot root” because of its similar taste.
In the 19th century parsnip was used as a sugar substitute in confectionery.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cooked parsnip provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance and normal heart function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Parsnip is virtually fat‑free, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Phenolic compounds in parsnip combat free radicals and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to parsnip, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Parsnip contains oxalates, which in high amounts can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Raw or poorly washed roots may carry soil contaminants; thorough washing and cooking are recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked parsnip can be served as a side dish, added to vegetable stews, mashed, mixed into salads, or used in casseroles. It also makes a smooth puree suitable for baby foods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh parsnips in a cool, dry place in a paper bag for 2‑3 weeks. Cooked parsnip keeps in the refrigerator in an airtight container for 3‑5 days. Discard if it develops a sour smell or soft, mushy spots.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-and-s.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce and Seafood, Ready‑to‑Heat

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with cream sauce and seafood is a ready‑to‑heat meal that can be quickly warmed in a microwave or on the stove. It contains whole‑grain pasta, a cream‑based sauce, and a mix of seafood such as shrimp, mussels, and squid. The dish provides complex carbohydrates, protein, and healthy fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta offers more fiber and micronutrients than refined white pasta.
The cream sauce is often made with a blend of dairy cream and a touch of olive oil for a lighter texture.
Seafood is an excellent source of omega‑3 fatty acids, which support heart health.
The meal is designed for fast preparation: only 3‑5 minutes in the microwave are needed.
Ready‑to‑heat seafood pasta dishes are popular in the “quick and healthy” segment of the market.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta supplies dietary fiber that promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Seafood adds complete protein essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Shrimp, mussels, and squid provide EPA and DHA, beneficial for heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the pasta and seafood contain B12, B6, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The cream sauce contributes calcium, while seafood supplies vitamin D, both important for bone health.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to shrimp, mussels, or squid may experience severe reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The prepared sauce can be high in salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The cream sauce contains dairy, which may be problematic for those with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Proper heating
items.content: Insufficient heating may leave harmful bacteria alive, so follow the recommended heating time.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the portion in the microwave for about 3‑5 minutes or on a skillet, stirring occasionally. Serve immediately; optionally garnish with fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or grated Parmesan cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen product in a freezer at –18 °C. Once thawed, consume within 24 hours. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese pizza with stuffed crust is a classic Italian-style pizza featuring a thin base topped with tomato sauce, a generous layer of mozzarella cheese, and baked to a golden finish. The distinctive feature is the stuffed crust, which is filled with extra cheese, making the edge especially crunchy and flavorful.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stuffed crust pizza first appeared in the United States in the 1980s as a response to consumer demand for a more "cheesy" pizza option.
The combination of tomato sauce and mozzarella is traditional to Naples, the birthplace of the classic Margherita.
Cheese in the stuffed rim is often blended with Parmesan or cheddar to boost flavor.
A stuffed‑crust pizza typically contains 15‑20 % more calories than a regular pizza of the same size.
In some countries the pizza is served with additional pesto or chipotle sauce on the side.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Mozzarella and other cheeses used in the stuffing provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium for bones
items.content: Cheeses are a good source of calcium, which supports strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tomatoes and cheese contain vitamins B2 and B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that may reduce the risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The mix of carbs from the crust, fats from the cheese, and protein makes the pizza filling and helps maintain fullness longer.

items.title: High calories and fat
items.content: The stuffed crust adds extra cheese, increasing overall calorie count and saturated fat content.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheeses and sauces often contain a lot of salt, which can be an issue for people with hypertension.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: For those who are lactose intolerant, cheese may cause discomfort; lactose‑free options are recommended.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, cutting it into individual slices. Fresh herbs such as basil or oregano, or a light arugula salad, add a bright contrast to the rich flavors.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill pan to keep the crust crispy.

content.title: About
content.content: A fish taco is a Mexican dish consisting of a soft corn or flour tortilla filled with grilled or baked fish, fresh vegetables, sauce, and spices. The fish is usually seasoned with lime, cilantro, and chili, giving the taco a bright aroma and a mild heat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White fish such as cod, snapper, or halibut is traditionally used in fish tacos.
Fish tacos became popular in coastal California in the 1980s.
Tortillas are often made from corn masa, making the dish naturally gluten‑free.
The combination of fish and lime reduces fishy odor and enhances flavor.
A common sauce for fish tacos is a creamy chipotle mayo or yogurt‑based dressing.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Fish provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA support heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Fish supplies B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Compared with meat‑based tacos, fish tacos are usually lower in calories when not overloaded with sauces.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Fish delivers selenium, iodine, and phosphorus, which aid thyroid function and bone health.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Certain fish species can contain mercury or other toxins; choose reputable sources.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Marinades and sauces can be salty, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Lime acidity
items.content: Large amounts of lime juice may irritate the stomach in people with gastritis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fish tacos hot, folding the tortilla in half and adding fish, fresh veggies (cabbage, tomato, avocado), sauce, and a squeeze of lime. Optional toppings include guacamole or salsa for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked fish in the refrigerator for up to 2 days in an airtight container. Keep tortilla dough in a cool, dry place, and pre‑made tortillas in a sealed bag at room temperature for up to 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Tongue is an edible meat product obtained from the muscular organ of beef cattle. It has a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a firm yet tender texture. Tongue is used in traditional dishes across many world cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tongue is considered a delicacy in many cultures, including French, Mexican, and Japanese cuisines.
In Russia, tongue is often served as a cold appetizer, marinated in vinegar and spices.
There is a tradition of preparing "tongue in batter" where the meat is coated in batter and fried.
Tongue is rich in collagen, which is often used in broths to improve their body.
In some countries, tongue is cooked in sauce, simmered with tomatoes and vegetables.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Tongue provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamins B12, B6 and niacin, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: The iron in tongue is readily absorbed and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Rich in zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Collagen content
items.content: Collagen supports skin, joint and connective‑tissue health.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Tongue contains a notable amount of saturated fat, so it should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Like any meat product, tongue can harbor pathogens if not stored or cooked properly.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef tongue.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: Tongue contains cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tongue is usually boiled until tender, then the outer skin is removed and it is sliced. It can be served hot as a stew, cold as sliced cold cuts, marinated, baked, or cooked in sauce. Common accompaniments include mustard, horseradish, or tomato‑based sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh tongue in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C in an airtight container for no more than 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze it at –18 °C in a sealed bag for up to 3 months. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or discoloration—signs of spoilage include sour smell and color change.
